idiom_name: Spring Integration claim-check-in / claim-check-out transformers over a MessageStore
implementation_notes: Spring Integration ships the pattern as a pair of transformers over a MessageStore strategy: claim-check-in persists the incoming message, indexes it with a generated UUID and replaces the payload with that id, and claim-check-out resolves the id back into the original message and, with remove-message=true, deletes it so the payload can be claimed exactly once. The store is the pluggable part - SimpleMessageStore is a Map for tests, JdbcMessageStore is durable, and implementing MessageStore is the extension point - so the classic hand-written form (write the body to a table or directory, put a UUID in a JMS header, fetch and delete in the consumer) is only justified when the service does not use Spring Integration and the transformation has to live inside existing JMS code.
code_sketch:
<int:claim-check-in id="checkin" input-channel="checkinChannel"
                    message-store="jdbcStore" output-channel="reduced"/>
<int:claim-check-out id="checkout" input-channel="checkoutChannel"
                     message-store="jdbcStore" remove-message="true"/>
<!-- remove-message=true claims the payload once; the default is repeatable redemption -->
pitfalls: The claim check is the payload of the transformed message, so a message that re-enters claim-check-in stores a token for a token - a mistake that is hard to see in a flow graph and turns redemption into a chain.

The store choice is a durability decision: SimpleMessageStore is an in-memory Map that grows until the JVM throws OutOfMemoryException and does not survive a restart, so production flows need JdbcMessageStore or an equivalent.
remove-message defaults to false, which makes redemption repeatable: every consumer that claims the check must be idempotent, because a redelivery will process the payload again.
Every node hosting the transformer must reach the same store; a partitioned or node-local store turns the pattern into a message-flow outage rather than a slow path.
